The claims a table of studies supports

Source: R/doc-claims-draw.R
gr_claims.Rd

Turns an extraction table into statements about the literature, each naming the studies it rests on. It is the step that makes a write-up a synthesis rather than an ordered recitation, and the step that lets a section be written from an argument instead of from rows.

Usage

gr_claims(
  extraction,
  question = NULL,
  protocol = NULL,
  client = NULL,
  model = NULL,
  temperature = NULL,
  max_claim_tokens = 1600L,
  include_unclear = FALSE,
  trace = NULL,
  bib = NULL,
  effort = NULL,
  unverified = c("exclude", "include"),
  moderators = NULL
)

Arguments

extraction

A gr_extract() result, or a data frame shaped like its $table.

question

The review question. Taken from protocol if omitted.

protocol

A gr_protocol(); its question is used when question is not given.

client

An hr_client(). One is built from model if omitted.

model, temperature, max_claim_tokens

Passed to the model call. max_claim_tokens is the reply limit for each call, and it also sets how many studies go into one: about (max_claim_tokens - 400) / 40. Raise it for fewer, larger batches.

include_unclear

Keep rows with nothing extracted. Off by default, the same as gr_synthesise().

trace

An hr_trace() to add this stage's calls to, or NULL. The calls are recorded on a trace of the stage's own, returned as $trace, and folded into trace when the stage ends, as in gr_read_many() and gr_synthesise(). Its requests are held to the governor of trace, if it has one, less what trace has already spent (see hr_governor()).

bib

Which columns carry bibliographic identity, as in gr_synthesise(): a named list of citation, authors, year, title, venue, doi. Those columns are withheld from the model, so a claim cannot attribute a finding to a name, and cannot be moderated by one. Omitted, only the conventional names are withheld. Pass the same bib to gr_synthesise() and gr_gaps().

effort

Reasoning effort, or NULL (the default) to send none: one string, or a character vector named by stage, as effort in gr_read_spec(). The calls here are labelled claims.draw and claims.reconcile, so c(claims = "high") covers both. Drawing claims is judgement, the stage most worth a higher effort. The reasoning counts against the same reply limit, so a high effort can leave a batch's reply cut off, which is reported as such (gr_claims_truncated).

unverified

What the claims prompt does with an extracted value whose quote did not verify, or that came with no quote (see gr_extract(), "Verifying it"). "exclude" (the default) leaves it out of the prompt, so no claim rests on it, and lists it in $unverified; "include" shows it, marked unverified with the quote that was given. Either way each value shown carries its check and its quote. Only a gr_extract() result carries the quotes: a bare table's values are shown as they are, with no check, and nothing is left out. The default is untested: it follows the rule that a claim should rest on what the documents were found to say, and no benchmark has compared the two.

moderators

The columns you expected, before reading, to explain a disagreement between studies: a character vector of column names, or NULL (the default) for none. A claim's moderator is "declared" when it is one of these, and is then tested with the others for multiplicity (Holm). Any other moderator the model names is "exploratory", and so is any split of one study against one. See "Moderators" below. Naming a column changes nothing that is sent.

Value

An object of class gr_claims:

claims

One row per claim: claim_id, claim, kind, moderator, moderator_status ("declared", "exploratory" or NA), scope, n_support, n_contradict, sign_p, low_power, note. sign_p is the exact two-sided sign test of the claim's direction tally, n_support of n_support + n_contradict studies: 5 of 5 gives 0.0625. low_power is TRUE when the tally is 5 studies or fewer, so that no split of it can reach p < 0.05. See "Direction of effect" below.

support

Long: claim_id, study, role ("supports" or "contradicts"). Join it to $studies to reach documents and quotes.

studies

The rows the claims were drawn from, numbered.

dropped

What verification removed, and why.

partial

TRUE when some studies contributed nothing because their batch was cut off at the reply limit, failed, or was not sent for a call or cost limit.

lost

The study numbers of those studies.

unmerged

TRUE when claims from several batches could not be reconciled, so one finding may appear as more than one claim.

hidden

The columns withheld from the model as bibliographic.

values

Each extracted value of the studies, one row per study and field: study, document, field, value, status ("verified", "unverified" or "not reported") and quote (the verified quote, else the closest one given, else NA). Empty for a bare table, which carries no quotes.

moderators

One row per claim that names a moderator: claim_id, moderator, declared, exploratory, n_support and n_contradict (the studies on each side that report it), fisher_p, min_p and holm_p. See "Moderators" below.

declared

The moderators named in advance that the model was shown.

unverified

The unverified values, listed apart: study, document, field, value, quote and shown, whether the prompt showed them (unverified = "include").

What makes a claim checkable

Every study number a claim names is verified against the table, exactly as a [study N] marker in finished prose already is, and against the batch the claim was drawn from: a claim may only name studies its call was shown. A number that fails either is dropped and counted rather than trusted, a claim left with no supporting study is dropped entirely, and a moderator naming a column the model was not shown is cleared: it is an invented explanation for a real disagreement. So is a moderator that does not tell the two sides of a contested claim apart by counting: a column the table does not report for the studies on one side, a value reported on both sides, or numbers whose ranges overlap. $dropped records all of it, so a claims table that looks thin can be told apart from a literature that is.

The study numbers are the same ones gr_synthesise() cites, because both derive them from one function. A claim resting on study 3 and a sentence citing [study 3] point at the same row by construction.

Corpora too large for one prompt

The studies are batched, and claims are then reconciled across batches in one further call that sees only the claim TEXTS. Without it a claim holding across the whole corpus comes back once per batch with disjoint support, which reads as several narrow claims instead of one broad one. The reconcile pass may only group claims that already exist: every claim it fails to place stays on its own rather than disappearing. When it cannot run (a call or cost limit, a failed or cut-off reply, a reply that is not a list of groups, or more claims than fit one prompt), the claims are kept unmerged, with a warning, and $unmerged is TRUE.

What the reconcile pass cannot check is MEANING. A merged claim keeps one member's wording and the union of every member's studies, so if the model groups two claims that say different things, the studies behind one are listed as supporting the other's wording. Two such errors are refused by reading words: findings that point different ways, and claims naming different populations (adults, children, adolescents, infants, older people, women, men, students), read from the claim and its scope, are kept apart whatever the reply grouped, with a warning (gr_claims_kept_apart) and a note. A finding is read on three axes: whether it states no effect ("has no effect on Y", "did not improve Y", "ineffective"), whether it names a benefit or a harm ("improves", "harms"), and whether it names a rise or a fall ("raises", "reduces"). Two findings are kept apart when one states no effect and the other one, or when both speak to the same axis and differ. "Improves depressive symptoms" and "reduces depressive symptoms" stay together, since a fall can be a benefit; for the same reason "improves Y" and "reduces Y" are not told apart. The words are English and the lists short, and a population outside the list is not recognised, so a merge they do not catch is still possible. The merged claim takes the wording of the member most studies support, then the one fewest contradict, then the first in a fixed order, not the longest, so the result does not depend on the order of the table. Its note names every other wording it absorbed so that it can be seen, and a group mixing claims of different kind is warned about.

A batch is limited by the reply as well as by the context window, because the reply names every study it uses: with the default max_claim_tokens a batch holds about 30 studies. A batch whose reply is cut off, or whose call fails, is reported with the number of studies it held rather than passed over.

Direction of effect

A claim's tally is a direction-of-effect count: how many of the studies it names point its way. Each claim carries the exact sign test of that count, the binomial probability of a split at least as uneven if each study were as likely to point either way (sign_p, two-sided), and claims are ranked by it, lowest p first, wherever they are ranked (print(), and the sentence budget gr_synthesise() gives each claim). A two-sided test is as small for a tally against the claim as for one in its favour (1 of 9 gives 0.039, below 5 of 5 at 0.0625), so a claim that more of its studies contradict than support ranks after every other claim, the least contradicted of those first. The number of studies voting was the rank before, which put a contested 3-to-3 claim above an agreed 5-of-5 one. A sign test is weak: with 5 studies or fewer no split, however even or uneven, can reach p < 0.05, and print() warns of low power. Read such a tally as a count of directions, not as evidence of an effect or of none. This follows SWiM's guidance on vote counting by direction of effect (Campbell et al. 2020, BMJ 368:l6890) and Boon and Thomson (2021, Research Synthesis Methods 12:29-33) on direction tallies and their sign test.

Moderators

A moderator is kept only when it separates a claim's supporting studies from its contradicting ones (see "What makes a claim checkable"). Kept, it is tested. fisher_p is Fisher's exact test, two-sided, of the 2 x 2 table of side (supports, contradicts) against which side's values a study has; min_p is the smallest p a table with those margins can give. Since a kept moderator splits the studies perfectly, the two are equal: the test says how much a split that clean can show with that few studies. One study on each side gives p = 1, which is why a 1-vs-1 split is always "exploratory": it is a coincidence as often as an explanation. For the moderators named in moderators, holm_p adjusts fisher_p for their number by Holm's method; an exploratory moderator has none, since the number of columns the model looked through is not known. The writing prompt marks an exploratory moderator as such.

These are between-study comparisons of direction, not tests of an interaction on effect sizes. Assess each moderator you rely on against the ICEMAN items for effect modification (Schandelmaier et al. 2020, CMAJ 192:E901-E906); harnessr scores none of them, and lists them, with what it reports on each, in the audit report:

  • Is the effect modification based on comparison within studies rather than between them? (Here it is between studies.)

  • Was the moderator specified before the analysis? (declared.)

  • Was the direction of the effect modification hypothesised in advance, and correctly?

  • Does a test for interaction suggest that chance is an unlikely explanation? (fisher_p tests directions only.)

  • Was only a small number of moderators tested, or was the number allowed for? (holm_p, over the declared ones.)

  • For a continuous moderator, were arbitrary cut points avoided?

  • Is the effect modification consistent across related outcomes?

See also

gr_outline() to derive sections from these claims, gr_synthesise() to write from them, gr_gaps() for what they do not cover, gr_protocols() for the claims schema they want as input

Examples

tab <- data.frame(
  document = c("a.pdf", "b.pdf"), status = "ok", duplicate_of = NA_character_,
  n_filled = 2L, n_unverified = 0L, conflicts = NA_character_,
  design = c("randomised trial", "cross-sectional"),
  finding = c("supports", "contradicts"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) paste0(
  '{"claims":[{"claim":"The effect appears in trials but not in surveys.",',
  '"kind":"finding","supported_by":[1],"contradicted_by":[2],',
  '"moderator":"design","scope":"one trial, one survey"}]}'))

cm <- gr_claims(tab, question = "Does it work?", client = cl)
cm$claims[, c("claim", "moderator", "n_support", "n_contradict")]
#>                                              claim moderator n_support
#> 1 The effect appears in trials but not in surveys.    design         1
#>   n_contradict
#> 1            1
cm$support
#>   claim_id study        role
#> 1        1     1    supports
#> 2        1     2 contradicts
